analysis.one_liner: Adds outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare with a deductible, payment limits, and pharmacy agreements.
analysis.headline: Introduced in 1999 and referred to two House committees, the bill never reached a vote and died when that Congress ended in January 2001, leaving Medicare still without outpatient drug coverage.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1999, Medicare paid hospital and doctor bills but covered almost no outpatient prescription drugs, so seniors paid full retail price at the pharmacy. This bill would have made Medicare a payer for outpatient drugs, covering 80% of the cost after a yearly deductible, paying pharmacies directly under participation agreements, and setting payment limits based on drug price surveys. It was a Democratic-sponsored starting proposal that never got past subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, then about 39 million seniors and disabled Americans, who in 1999 had no Medicare coverage for outpatient prescription drugs and paid out of pocket. The bill would have covered 80% of drug costs after a $250 deductible starting in 2001, and required participating pharmacies to counsel beneficiaries on drug interactions and cheaper therapeutic equivalents, and to charge seniors no more than the general public.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would begin paying 80% of covered outpatient drug costs after a $250 annual deductible, starting in 2001, covering prescription drugs, biologics, and insulin.
The bill would bar the Secretary of Health and Human Services from creating a formulary to exclude specific drugs or specific uses, except on safety or effectiveness grounds.

Participating pharmacies would have to counsel Medicare beneficiaries on drug use and interactions, advise them on therapeutically equivalent alternatives, and could not charge beneficiaries more than the general public.
The bill would create a Prescription Drug Payment Review Commission to report annually to Congress on how drug payments are set.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund and Medicare Part B, which would take on an entirely new category of spending. Pharmacies would accept assignment-based payment plus a small dispensing allowance, and the Secretary would be barred from using formularies to steer volume toward cheaper drugs, which raises the bill's cost.

drawbacks.text: After the $250 deductible, beneficiaries would still pay 20% of drug costs with no annual out-of-pocket maximum, so the very large drug bills that hit the sickest patients hardest would not be capped.

Payment limits would be set from average wholesale price surveys plus a dispensing allowance, and the bill would forbid formularies, so the government would pay list-based prices rather than negotiating discounts or steering patients to cheaper drugs.
The deductible would rise every year along with Medicare Part B premium increases, so the fixed-dollar protection would erode over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This would have been the first broad federal drug coverage for Medicare beneficiaries, a real protection for people then paying full retail price for medications. But the design left serious gaps: no cap on yearly out-of-pocket spending, payment limits based on list prices rather than negotiated discounts, and an explicit prohibition on formularies, all of which would have made the benefit expensive for taxpayers while leaving the costliest cases partly exposed. It was an opening bid in the 1999 drug-coverage debate, and it was never amended or improved because no committee ever acted on it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and then to their health subcommittees, and no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the Medicare Outpatient Prescription Drug Coverage Act on March 15, 1999, with eight New York colleagues as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
In late March and early April 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Health and Environment Subcommittee and the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, the last recorded action.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The bill would have added coverage of outpatient prescription drugs to Medicare Part B, with payment rules, a $250 deductible, payment limits, and civil-money-penalty enforcement against pharmacies that overcharge.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing in that Congress and continued paying full retail price for prescriptions. Drug manufacturers kept selling to seniors at unrestricted retail prices with no government payment limits, and the debate over who would deliver a drug benefit — a government program like this bill, or private insurers — stayed open until a private-insurer design passed in 2003.

for.name: Rep. Eliot Engel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 15, 1999 and recruited eight New York colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: 25 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Commerce Committee and Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the two committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill's last recorded action was subcommittee referral in April 1999.

against.name: House Republican majority leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Pursued its own Medicare drug-coverage proposals instead and never brought this bill to the floor.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Ran national advertising opposing Medicare drug plans that set government payment limits, urging a private-coverage approach instead.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 supporters — the sponsor and 25 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the Republican-majority committees that controlled the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: Medicare would become a new, enormous paying customer for their products, and the bill would bar the government from using formularies to push cheaper alternatives — but Medicare's payments would be capped by survey-based payment limits rather than open-ended charges. Their interest in the new demand runs alongside beneficiaries', while their resistance to payment limits ran against taxpayers.

Participating pharmacies would get a guaranteed federal payer, a dispensing allowance per prescription, a distinctive emblem, and government-provided electronic claims equipment. In exchange they would accept assignment, counsel beneficiaries, and could not charge seniors more than the general public.

The bill would keep private prepaid plans inside the drug benefit, letting them integrate coverage while requiring them to track enrollees' drug expenses toward the Medicare deductible and to make special 'drug buy-out' arrangements. It preserves their role rather than displacing it.
